questions.answer:
## Next.js (App Router)

Export a `metadata` object from each `page.js` (or `layout.js`) with its own `title` and `description` [4]:

```tsx
// app/about/page.tsx
import type { Metadata } from 'next'

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: 'About',
  description: 'About Acme...',
}

export default function Page() {}
```

Metadata from multiple segments in a route is shallowly merged, and a page's `title` replaces the one from the layout [1][2]. Nested fields like `openGraph` are replaced as a whole if the page sets them, so share common nested values through a separate variable if needed [2].

The docs also mention a `generateMetadata` function as an alternative to the `metadata` object [5], but the provided passages don't show how to use it.

## Angular

Angular's routing docs cover page titles only. Set a `title` on each route, and Angular updates the page title when the route activates [3]:

```ts
const routes: Routes = [
  { path: '', component: Home, title: 'Home Page' },
  { path: 'about', component: About, title: 'About Us' },
];
```

You can also set the title dynamically with a `ResolveFn`, or through a service extending `TitleStrategy` [3].

The provided Angular docs don't cover setting a meta description per page.

questions.question: How do I read a cookie inside a server component?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I read a cookie inside a server component?

retrieved.headingPath: cookies

questions.answer:
Use the async `cookies` function from `next/headers` and `await` it, then call `.get()` on the returned store:

```tsx
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'

export default async function Page() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies()
  const theme = cookieStore.get('theme')
  return '...'
}
```
[1]

Reading works in Server Components because the browser sends cookie data to the server in the HTTP request headers. [5]

Things to keep in mind:

- **Setting or deleting isn't supported during Server Component rendering.** Use a Server Function or a Route Handler for that. [5]
- **Don't call `cookies()` inside an `after` callback** in a Server Component, as it throws a runtime error. Read the value beforehand and pass it in. [2]

```tsx
const sessionCookie = (await cookies()).get('session-id')?.value || 'anonymous'

after(() => {
  logUserAction({ sessionCookie })
})
```
[2]

- **With Cache Components**, a component that reads `cookies` must be wrapped in `<Suspense>` so the rest of the page can be prerendered into a static shell. [2]

questions.searchedQuestion: After a server action saves a new post, how do I make the posts list show it in Next.js?

retrieved.headingPath: updateTag > Examples > Server Action with Read-Your-Own-Writes

questions.answer:
After the mutation in your Server Action, invalidate the cache so the list re-renders with fresh data. There are two main options.

## Option 1: `updateTag` (read-your-own-writes)

Use this when the user should see their change immediately. It expires the tagged data right away, and it can only be called from a Server Action [5].

```ts
'use server'

import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'

export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  const post = await db.post.create({
    data: {
      title: formData.get('title'),
      content: formData.get('content'),
    },
  })

  updateTag('posts')
  redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`)
}
```
[5]

The `'posts'` tag should affect any page that displays a list of posts. You can also invalidate a per-post tag such as `` `post-${post.id}` `` for the detail page [1]. With Cache Components, tag the data using `cacheTag` inside a `use cache` function rather than the `fetch` `next.tags` option [4].

## Option 2: `revalidatePath`

If you'd rather invalidate by route, call `revalidatePath` after the mutation [2]:

```ts
'use server'

import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  // Mutate data
  // ...

  revalidatePath('/posts')
}
```
[2]

## What happens on the client

When the action calls `updateTag` or `revalidatePath`, Next.js re-renders the current route in the same HTTP response as the action. You don't need a follow-up fetch to see the updated UI [3]. Calling `redirect` also streams the destination's RSC Payload in that response [3].

## Which to pick

- `updateTag`: immediately expires the cache; Server Actions only [5].
- `revalidateTag`: stale-while-revalidate, for cases where a slight delay is OK; works in Server Actions and Route Handlers [5]. It requires a cache profile as the second argument, such as `'max'` [4].

questions.searchedQuestion: How do I expose an environment variable to code running in the browser?

retrieved.headingPath: How to use environment variables in Next.js > Bundling Environment Variables for the Browser
How to use environment variables in Next.js > Bundling Environment Variables for the Browser > Runtime Environment Variables
How to self-host your Next.js application > Environment Variables
env
How to migrate from Create React App to Next.js > Migration Steps > Step 9: Migrate Environment Variables

questions.answer:
Prefix the variable name with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. Without that prefix, environment variables are only available on the server (Node.js) [1][2].

```txt filename=".env"
NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID=abcdefghijk
```

Next.js inlines the value at build time into the JavaScript bundle sent to the browser, replacing references to `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID` with the value from the environment where you run `next build` [1].

```js filename="pages/index.js"
import setupAnalyticsService from '../lib/my-analytics-service'

// It will be transformed at build time to `setupAnalyticsService('abcdefghijk')`.
setupAnalyticsService(process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID)
```

**Caveats**
- The values are frozen at build time. After the build, the app no longer responds to changes in these variables. If you need runtime values in the browser, you have to set up your own API to provide them to the client [1].
- Dynamic lookups are not inlined [1]. The docs provided cut off before showing the example.

**Alternative: `env` in `next.config.js`**

You can also add variables to the bundle through the `env` config. These are always included in the bundle, and the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix has no effect on them [4].

```js filename="next.config.js"
module.exports = {
  env: {
    customKey: 'my-value',
  },
}
```

Destructuring `process.env` variables won't work with this approach [4].

**Migrating from Create React App:** rename `REACT_APP_` variables to `NEXT_PUBLIC_` [5].

retrieved.headingPath: How to set up Jest with Next.js > Manual setup

questions.answer:
You can either start from the official example or set Jest up manually.

## Quickstart

Use `create-next-app` with the `with-jest` example:

```bash
npx create-next-app@latest --example with-jest with-jest-app
```
[4]

## Manual setup

**1. Install dev dependencies:**

```bash
npm install -D jest jest-environment-jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/dom @testing-library/jest-dom ts-node @types/jest
```
[1]

**2. Generate a basic Jest config** (this prompts you through setup and creates `jest.config.ts|js`):

```bash
npm init jest@latest
```
[1]

**3. Update the config to use `next/jest`**, which has the necessary configuration for Jest to work with Next.js:

```ts
import type { Config } from 'jest'
import nextJest from 'next/jest.js'

const createJestConfig = nextJest({
  // Provide the path to your Next.js app to load next.config.js and .env files in your test environment
  dir: './',
})

// Add any custom config to be passed to Jest
const config: Config = {
  coverageProvider: 'v8',
  testEnvironment: 'jsdom',
  // Add more setup options before each test is run
  // setupFilesAfterEnv: ['<rootDir>/jest.setup.ts'],
}

// createJestConfig is exported this way to ensure that next/jest can load the Next.js config which is async
export default createJestConfig(config)
```
[2]

`next/jest` automatically sets up `transform` with the Next.js Compiler, mocks stylesheets, image imports and `next/font`, loads `.env` files into `process.env`, ignores `node_modules` and `.next`, and loads `next.config.js` [2].

**4. Add test scripts to `package.json`:**

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "jest",
    "test:watch": "jest --watch"
  }
}
```
[3]

`jest --watch` re-runs tests when a file changes [3].

**5. Write a test.** Create a `__tests__` folder in the project root [3], then add a test such as:

```jsx
import '@testing-library/jest-dom'
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react'
import Page from '../app/page'

describe('Page', () => {
  it('renders a heading', () => {
    render(<Page />)

    const heading = screen.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })

    expect(heading).toBeInTheDocument()
  })
})
```
[3]

Then run `npm test` (the `test` script from step 4).

**Note:** To test environment variables directly, load them manually in a separate setup script or in your `jest.config.ts` file [2].

questions.question: What's the difference between toBe and toEqual?
questions.searchedQuestion: What's the difference between toBe and toEqual?

retrieved.headingPath: Using Matchers > Common Matchers
Using Matchers > Numbers
Expect > Matchers > .toEqual(value)
Expect > Matchers > .toBe(value)
Expect > Extend Utilities > expect.extend(matchers)

questions.answer:
**`toBe`** checks exact equality using `Object.is`. Use it for primitive values or to check referential identity of object instances [1][4].

**`toEqual`** recursively compares all fields of an object or array ("deep" equality). It uses `Object.is` for primitive values [1][3].

The docs' example shows the difference. Two separate objects with the same properties pass `toEqual` but fail `toBe`, because they aren't the same instance:

```js
const can1 = {flavor: 'grapefruit', ounces: 12};
const can2 = {flavor: 'grapefruit', ounces: 12};

expect(can1).toEqual(can2);   // passes
expect(can1).not.toBe(can2);  // passes: not the exact same object
```
[3]

**Other details:**
- For numbers, `toBe` and `toEqual` are equivalent [2]. For floating-point numbers, use `toBeCloseTo` instead of either [2][4].
- `toEqual` ignores object keys with `undefined` properties, `undefined` array items, array sparseness, and object type mismatch. Use `toStrictEqual` if you want those taken into account [1][3].
- `toEqual` doesn't deep-compare errors. Only the `message` property is considered, and the docs recommend `.toThrow` for testing errors [3].
- `toBe` checks referential identity but reports a deep comparison of values when it fails [4].

questions.answer:
Run Jest with the `--updateSnapshot` flag (alias `-u`) to re-generate the snapshot artifacts:

```bash
jest --updateSnapshot
# or
jest -u
```

This re-records every snapshot that fails during that run [1][2]. Before doing this, fix any failures caused by real bugs. Otherwise you'll record snapshots of the buggy behavior [1]. Also inspect each failure to confirm the change is intended [4].

**Limit which snapshots get updated:** Pass `--testNamePattern` to re-record only the matching tests. The flag can also be combined with a test suite pattern [1][2].

**Update interactively:** In watch mode, Interactive Snapshot Mode steps you through the failed snapshots one test at a time. You can review each failed output and choose to update it or skip to the next [3].

Commit the updated snapshot files along with your code changes [4].

Use the `-t` (alias `--testNamePattern`) CLI option with a regex:

```bash
jest -t name-of-spec
```

This matches against the name in `describe` or `test` [3]. For example, to run only authorization tests with names like `'GET /api/posts with auth'`:

```bash
jest -t=auth
```

The regex is matched against the full name, which combines the test name and all its surrounding `describe` block names [1].

If you only want to narrow by file rather than test name, pass a regex or path to `jest` (e.g. `jest path/to/my-test.js`) [3][4], or use `--testPathPatterns` [5].

To focus on specific tests within a single file while debugging, you can use `test.only` instead, though you usually shouldn't commit it to source control [2].

questions.question: Whats the best way to render a really long scrolling list?
questions.searchedQuestion: What's the best way to render a really long scrolling list?

retrieved.headingPath: Using List Views
Core Components and APIs > List Views
ScrollView

Performance Overview > Common sources of performance problems > FlatList rendering is too slow or scroll performance is bad for large lists

questions.answer:
Use `FlatList` (or `SectionList` if your data is split into sections with headers).

**Why not `ScrollView`:** `ScrollView` renders all its children at once, which slows rendering and increases memory usage for long lists [3]. `FlatList` renders items lazily as they're about to appear and removes items that scroll far off screen, saving memory and processing time [3]. Only elements currently showing on screen are rendered [1][2].

**Basic usage:** `FlatList` requires two props: `data` (the source of information) and `renderItem` (takes one item and returns a component to render) [1].

```jsx
import {FlatList, Text} from 'react-native';

<FlatList
  data={[{key: 'Devin'}, {key: 'Dan'}, {key: 'Dominic'}]}
  renderItem={({item}) => <Text>{item.key}</Text>}
/>
```

**Sectioned data:** Use `SectionList` if you want data broken into logical sections with headers [1][2].

**If it's still slow:**
- Implement [`getItemLayout`](https://reactnative.dev/docs/flatlist#getitemlayout) so rendering can skip measuring items [5].
- Consider third-party list libraries optimized for performance, such as FlashList or Legend List [5].
- If you need more flexibility than `FlatList` offers (e.g. immutable data instead of plain arrays), `VirtualizedList` is the base implementation underneath it [4].

`FlatList` also supports separators, multiple columns, and infinite scroll loading out of the box [3].

questions.answer:
Use React Native's `Appearance` module, or preferably the `useColorScheme` hook, which the docs recommend. [5]

**With the hook (recommended):**

The `useColorScheme` hook returns `'light'`, `'dark'`, or `null` (the latter may be returned if the native Appearance module isn't available). [4]

**With `Appearance.getColorScheme()`:**

```tsx
const colorScheme = Appearance.getColorScheme();
if (colorScheme === 'dark') {
  // Use dark color scheme
}
```
[5]

Notes:

- The value can change at runtime, for example from a scheduled sunrise/sunset change at the system level, or when the app overrides it via `setColorScheme()`. [1]
- Because of that, call `getColorScheme()` on every render rather than caching the value. [5]
- To react to changes, `Appearance.addChangeListener()` fires when appearance preferences change. On iOS and Android, the callback's `colorScheme` is always `'light'` or `'dark'`. [3]
- If the app has called `setColorScheme('light' | 'dark')`, the returned value reflects that override, not the system setting. Passing `'auto'` removes the override and restores the system preference. [5]

The docs provided don't include a usage example for the `useColorScheme` hook itself, only its return values.

questions.question: How do I get the screen width so my layout updates when it rotates?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I get the screen width so my layout updates when it rotates?

retrieved.headingPath: Dimensions
useWindowDimensions
useWindowDimensions > Properties > width
useWindowDimensions > Example
Dimensions > Reference > Methods > get()

questions.answer:
Use the `useWindowDimensions` hook. It automatically updates its values when the screen size or font scale changes, so your component re-renders on rotation. [2]

```tsx
import {useWindowDimensions} from 'react-native';

const {height, width} = useWindowDimensions();
```
[2]

`width` is the width in pixels of the window or screen your app occupies. [3]

The docs call `useWindowDimensions` the preferred API for React components, because unlike `Dimensions`, it updates as the window's dimensions update. [1]

If you use `Dimensions.get('window')` instead, the values can change (e.g. on rotation or on foldable devices), so don't cache them. Read them on every render, for example with inline styles rather than values set in a `StyleSheet`. [1] For devices that can change screen or window size, the docs also mention an event listener in the `Dimensions` module, but the provided context doesn't include its example or API details. [1]

questions.question: What should I use for a button that changes style while it's pressed?
questions.searchedQuestion: What should I use for a button that changes style while it's pressed?

retrieved.headingPath: Pressable > Example
Pressable > Props > style
Handling Touches > Touchables
Toolbar > Overview
Toolbar > Examples > Basic horizontal toolbar

questions.answer:
Use **`Pressable`** in React Native. Its `style` prop accepts a function that receives `{pressed}`, a boolean saying whether the component is currently pressed, and returns view styles [2]. Its children can also be a function of `{pressed}`, so the content can change too [1].

```jsx
<Pressable
  onPress={() => setTimesPressed(current => current + 1)}
  style={({pressed}) => [
    {
      backgroundColor: pressed ? 'rgb(210, 230, 255)' : 'white',
    },
    styles.wrapperCustom,
  ]}>
  {({pressed}) => (
    <Text style={styles.text}>{pressed ? 'Pressed!' : 'Press Me'}</Text>
  )}
</Pressable>
```
[1]

The docs also describe the "Touchable" components, which give built-in pressed feedback but no default styling [3]:

- **TouchableHighlight** darkens the view's background on press.
- **TouchableOpacity** reduces the button's opacity on press.
- **TouchableNativeFeedback** shows ink ripples on Android.
- **TouchableWithoutFeedback** shows no feedback.

[3]

The context doesn't say which one is preferred for new code. `Pressable` is the one shown with a style that depends directly on the pressed state.

questions.question: why do my views stack vertically by default instead of side by side?
questions.searchedQuestion: Why do my views stack vertically by default instead of side by side?

retrieved.headingPath: VirtualizedList > Reference > Props > horizontal
FlatList > Reference > Props > horizontal
Layout with Flexbox > Flex Direction
Layout Props > Reference > Props > flexDirection
ScrollView > Reference > Props > horizontal

questions.answer:
Views stack vertically because React Native's `flexDirection` defaults to `column`, which lays children out from top to bottom [3]. This differs from CSS, where `flex-direction` defaults to `row` [4].

To place children side by side, set `flexDirection: 'row'` on the parent container. This aligns children from left to right [3]. The other accepted values are `row-reverse`, `column`, and `column-reverse` [4].

```jsx
<View style={{ flexDirection: 'row' }}>
  <View />
  <View />
</View>
```

If you're using a list or scroll container, there's also a `horizontal` prop:

- `FlatList`: `horizontal={true}` renders items next to each other instead of stacked vertically [2].
- `ScrollView`: `horizontal` arranges children in a row instead of a column. It defaults to `false` [5].

questions.question: What is Hermes and do I need to enable it?
questions.searchedQuestion: What is Hermes and do I need to enable it?

retrieved.headingPath: Using Hermes
Optimizing JavaScript loading > Recommended: Use Hermes
JavaScript Environment > JavaScript Runtime
Using Hermes > Confirming Hermes is in use
Using Hermes > Bundled Hermes

questions.answer:
Hermes is an open-source JavaScript engine optimized for React Native. For many apps it improves start-up time, decreases memory usage, and reduces app size compared to JavaScriptCore. [1]

You don't need to enable it. React Native uses Hermes by default and no additional configuration is required. [1] It's the default engine for new React Native apps. [2]

Some related details:

- **Bundled version:** React Native ships with a bundled version of Hermes, built for each React Native release so the two stay compatible. [5]
- **Disabling:** If Hermes is disabled, React Native falls back to JavaScriptCore. [3] The docs say you can disable it with a command described on the Hermes page, but the passage provided doesn't include that command. [5]
- **Verifying it's in use:** Check for the `HermesInternal` global: [4]

```jsx
const isHermes = () => !!global.HermesInternal;
```

- **Release builds:** JavaScript is compiled to bytecode ahead of time, and the bytecode is loaded into memory on demand without needing to be parsed. [2] If you load the JS bundle in a non-standard way, `HermesInternal` may be available even though you aren't getting the pre-compiled bytecode, so confirm you're using the `.hbc` file. [4]

questions.question: How do I generate a signed release build for the Google Play Store?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I generate a signed release build for the Google Play Store?

retrieved.headingPath: Publishing to Google Play Store > Adding signing config to your app's Gradle config
Publishing to Google Play Store > Generating the release AAB
Publishing to Google Play Store
Publishing to Google Play Store > Generating an upload key
Publishing to Google Play Store > Testing the release build of your app

questions.answer:
Generating a signed release build involves these steps. The context doesn't show the step of adding the keystore credentials to `gradle.properties`, which the signing config below depends on (see the note at the end).

## 1. Generate an upload key

Use `keytool` to create a private signing key. On Windows, run it from `C:\Program Files\Java\jdkx.x.x_x\bin` as administrator:

```shell
keytool -genkeypair -v -storetype PKCS12 -keystore my-upload-key.keystore -alias my-key-alias -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
```

On macOS, find the JDK directory with `/usr/libexec/java_home`, `cd` into it, and run keytool with sudo:

```shell
sudo keytool -genkey -v -keystore my-upload-key.keystore -alias my-key-alias -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
```

Note the alias, since you'll use it when signing, and keep the keystore file private. [4]

## 2. Add the signing config to Gradle

Edit `android/app/build.gradle`:

```groovy
...
android {
    ...
    defaultConfig { ... }
    signingConfigs {
        release {
            if (project.hasProperty('MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE')) {
                storeFile file(MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE)
                storePassword MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_PASSWORD
                keyAlias MYAPP_UPLOAD_KEY_ALIAS
                keyPassword MYAPP_UPLOAD_KEY_PASSWORD
            }
        }
    }
    buildTypes {
        release {
            ...
            signingConfig signingConfigs.release
        }
    }
}
...
```
[1]

## 3. Generate the release AAB

```shell
npx react-native build-android --mode=release
```

This uses Gradle's `bundleRelease` to bundle the JavaScript into the AAB. Make sure `gradle.properties` does not include `org.gradle.configureondemand=true`, because that makes the release build skip bundling JS and assets. [2]

The output is at `android/app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab`, ready to upload to Google Play. [2]

Google Play must have App Signing by Google Play configured in the Play Console to accept the AAB format. [2]

## 4. Test the release build (recommended)

Uninstall any previous version of the app, then run one of these from the project root:

```shell
npm run android -- --mode="release"
```

```shell
yarn android --mode release
```

`--mode release` is only available if signing is set up as above. [5]

**Not covered:** the provided docs don't show where the `MYAPP_UPLOAD_*` properties get defined (for example, in `gradle.properties`), so I can't say how to set them from this context.

questions.question: How do I make a value that's derived from other signals?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I make a value that's derived from other signals?

retrieved.headingPath: Angular Signals > What are signals? > Computed signals
Signals > Computed expressions
Signal write in a disallowed context > Writing to signals is not allowed in a computed
Dependent state with linkedSignal
Angular Signals > Advanced derivations

questions.answer:
Use the `computed` function. It creates a read-only signal whose value is derived from other signals:

```typescript
const count: WritableSignal<number> = signal(0);
const doubleCount: Signal<number> = computed(() => count() * 2);
```
[1]

When any signal read inside the derivation changes, the computed value updates automatically:

```typescript
import {signal, computed} from '@angular/core';

const firstName = signal('Morgan');
const firstNameCapitalized = computed(() => firstName().toUpperCase());
console.log(firstNameCapitalized()); // MORGAN

firstName.set('Jaime');
console.log(firstNameCapitalized()); // JAIME
```
[2]

**Things to know:**

- **Lazy and memoized:** the derivation doesn't run until the first read. The result is cached and only recalculated after a dependency changes, so expensive derivations like filtering arrays are safe. [1]
- **Read-only:** a computed signal has no `set` or `update`. Calling `doubleCount.set(3)` is a compilation error. [1][2]
- **Dynamic dependencies:** only signals actually read during the derivation are tracked. [1]
- **No side effects:** writing to a signal inside a `computed` is not allowed (error NG0600). Derive the value instead of storing it in a separate signal and setting it. [3]

**If you need the derived value to be writable**, use `linkedSignal`. You pass a computation function like with `computed`, and the signal resets to the computation result when it changes, but you can still `set` it. [3][4]

```ts
selectedOption = linkedSignal(() => this.shippingOptions()[0]);
```
[4]

questions.question: How do I lazy load a page component with the router?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I lazy load a page component with the router?

retrieved.headingPath: Route Loading Strategies > Lazily loaded components and routes
Migration to lazy-loaded routes > How does it work?
Route Loading Strategies > Injection context lazy loading
Programmatically rendering components > Lazy-loading components
How to lazy load Client Components and libraries

questions.answer:
The question doesn't name a framework, but the context covers lazy-loaded routes for Angular's router, so here is that approach.

Use the `loadComponent` property on a route. It lazily loads the component's JavaScript when the route becomes active. [1]

```ts
import {Routes} from '@angular/router';

export const routes: Routes = [
  {
    path: 'login',
    loadComponent: () => import('./components/auth/login-page'),
  },
];
```
[1]

Key points:

- `loadComponent` takes a loader function that returns a Promise resolving to a component. Usually this is a standard dynamic `import()`, but any async loader function works. [1]
- If the file uses a `default` export, you can return the `import()` promise directly. Otherwise, select the exported class with `.then`: [1][2]

```ts
{
  path: 'home',
  loadComponent: () => import('./home').then((m) => m.Home),
}
```
[2]

- To lazy load child routes, use `loadChildren`, which loads them during route matching. [1]
- The loader runs in the route's injection context, so you can call `inject()` inside it, for example to choose which component to load. [3]
- Lazy loading moves code out of the initial bundle into separate chunks that the router requests only when the user visits the route. [1]

The context also describes a migration schematic that converts eagerly loaded standalone components in routes to `loadComponent`. [2]

If you meant Next.js or another framework, the docs provided don't cover router-based lazy loading for those.
